abstract: This study examines barriers preventing jobseekers from pursuing reskilling in high-demand occupations, using a discrete choice experiment with Italian jobseekers. The key finding is that perceived 'identity fit' — whether a new skill feels compatible with a person's sense of self — is the most important factor shaping reskilling decisions, often outweighing beliefs about monetary returns or employer demand.
keyFindings: Perceived identity fit in the target occupation is the most important individual-level factor shaping reskilling decisions
Willingness to pay estimates show participants are willing to pay to reskill into IT but would require compensation to reskill into construction
Beliefs about monetary returns and social status help explain differences in reskilling demand
A light-touch randomized information intervention providing data on occupational returns significantly increases reskilling interest
The information intervention also increased actual engagement in real-world training
methodology: Discrete choice experiment with real-world Italian jobseekers examining willingness to reskill into two high-demand occupations (IT assistant and construction technician). Includes a randomized information intervention. Published as NBER Working Paper 34633 and CEPR Discussion Paper 21055.
qualifiers: Study focuses on Italian jobseekers; labor market context may differ from the US. Reskilling is studied for two specific occupations (IT assistant and construction technician). Study is about general reskilling barriers, not AI-specific retraining.
